cues.text: A point in the Cartesian plane is specified by an ordered pair of real
coordinates.
The first coordinate measures horizontal position and the second measures
vertical position relative to perpendicular axes with the same length scale.
To find the distance between two points, subtract their x coordinates,
subtract
their y coordinates, square both differences, add, and take the nonnegative
square root.
For A at negative one, two and B at three, five, the horizontal change is four
and the vertical change is three.
The distance is square root of sixteen plus nine, or five.
Reversing the point order negates both differences but leaves their squares
unchanged.
A distance of zero means the two points coincide.
Squared distances are often easier to compare than distances because they
avoid
radicals without changing the comparison of nonnegative lengths.
The distance formula also tests a right angle through the converse of the
Pythagorean theorem.
Label the points and coordinates before substituting; confusing an x
coordinate
with a y coordinate changes the geometric problem rather than merely its
notation.
The section formula locates a point using its ratio along a segment.
If P divides A B internally with A P to P B equal to m to n, use positive
weights n on A and m on B, divided by m plus n.
The reversed placement of the two weights follows from the geometry: a larger
A
P means P is closer to B.
With A at zero, zero and B at six, three, internal ratio two to one gives P at
four, two.
Equal weights give the midpoint, three, three halves.
For external division with the same positive distance ratio m to n, the
formula
is the quantity m B minus n A divided by m minus n.
Ratio two to one in this example gives twelve, six, beyond B.
External equal ratios do not give a finite point when A and B are distinct,
because the denominator vanishes.
Check an answer by calculating the two distances and locating the point on the
correct line.
State whether division is internal or external before choosing the sign in the
formula.
A locus is the set of all points satisfying a stated geometric condition.
Start by calling a general moving point x, y and translating the condition
into
an equation.
If the point is equally distant from A at negative two, zero and B at two,
zero, equate the squared distances.
The equation is the square of x plus two plus y squared equal to the square of
x minus two plus y squared.
Expanding and cancelling gives eight x equal to zero, so the locus is x equal
to zero, the perpendicular bisector of A B.
Here squaring the two distances is equivalent because both sides are
nonnegative.
Other radical equations can gain extraneous points when squared, so check the
original condition and any domain restrictions afterward.
A locus includes all points satisfying the condition, not merely a few plotted
examples.
For a fixed distance r greater than zero from a point h, k, the same distance
formula gives the circle with equation the square of x minus h plus the square
of y minus k equal to r squared.
The slope of a nonvertical line is its change in y divided by its change in x.
Through one, two and three, six, the slope is four over two, or two.
Distinct parallel nonvertical lines have equal slopes.
Perpendicular nonvertical lines with finite slopes have product negative one,
so a line perpendicular to slope two has slope negative one half.
Do not use that product formula when a slope is undefined.
A vertical line x equal to a constant has no finite slope, while a horizontal
line has slope zero; those two directions are perpendicular.
If a line makes angle theta with the positive x axis, its slope is tangent
theta whenever that tangent is defined.
A line direction is unchanged by adding pi to its angle.
For general equations A x plus B y plus C equal to zero with B nonzero, the
slope is negative A over B.
The coefficients A and B cannot both vanish in a genuine line.
A sketch helps distinguish an undefined vertical slope from a zero horizontal
slope, but the equation supplies the exact test.
A point and a slope determine a nonvertical line through the point slope
equation y minus y one equal to m times x minus x one.
At point two, negative one with slope three, this gives y plus one equal to
three times x minus two, or y equal to three x minus seven.
Substituting the given point checks the constant term.
Two distinct points determine a line even when it is vertical.
A cross multiplied two point form avoids dividing by the horizontal
difference:
y minus y one times x two minus x one equals y two minus y one times
x minus x one.
Through one, two and three, six, it simplifies to y equal to two x.
If the points coincide, the condition does not determine a unique line.
The general form A x plus B y plus C equal to zero includes both vertical
and horizontal lines when A and B are not both zero.
Different nonzero multiples of the same triple of coefficients represent the
same line, so compare equations after allowing for a common scale factor.
A line meeting both axes at nonzero finite intercepts a and b has intercept
form x over a plus y over b equal to one.
Setting y equal to zero gives its x intercept, and setting x equal to zero
gives its y intercept.
For x over three plus y over four equal to one, the intercept points are
three,
zero and zero, four.
Multiplication gives four x plus three y minus twelve equal to zero.
Its normal vector has length five, so division by five yields four fifths x
plus three fifths y equal to twelve fifths.
This is normal form: the coefficients are cosine alpha and sine alpha for the
direction of a unit normal, and the nonnegative right hand side p is the
distance from the origin.
If the right hand side is negative, reverse the signs to use the convention p
nonnegative.
A line through the origin has p zero.
The usual intercept expression is unsuitable when an intercept is zero or
absent, so use the general or point form in those cases instead of dividing by
zero.
Intersecting lines share a point satisfying both equations.
Solve the pair x plus y equal to five and x minus y equal to one.
Adding gives two x equal to six, hence x is three and y is two.
Three lines are concurrent at a finite point when the same point lies on all
three.
For the additional line three x plus y equal to k, substitution of three, two
gives k equal to eleven.
This direct method makes the finite common point explicit.
A determinant condition for three line coefficients can be useful, but a zero
determinant alone can also occur for parallel arrangements and must be
interpreted with care.
Two general lines have a unique intersection when the determinant of their x
and y coefficients is nonzero.
If that determinant vanishes, check whether the lines are coincident or
distinct and parallel.
Identical equations after scaling describe one line, not a unique intersection
point.
When a parameter is present, do not divide by it before checking the value at
which the divisor vanishes.
Verify the computed coordinates in all the original equations.
Two intersecting lines generally make supplementary angles.
Unless another angle is requested, the smaller angle is between zero and pi
over two.
For finite slopes m one and m two, its tangent is the absolute value of m two
minus m one divided by one plus their product.
Slopes one and zero therefore give tangent theta equal to one, so theta is pi
over four.
If the denominator is zero, the lines are perpendicular and the smaller angle
is pi over two; a division by zero is not a finite tangent value.
A method that also handles vertical lines uses their normal vectors.
For general coefficients A one, B one and A two, B two, the cosine of the
smaller angle is the absolute value of the dot product divided by the product
of the normal lengths.
The absolute value removes the arbitrary reversal of a normal vector.
Normals with zero dot product correspond to perpendicular lines, while
proportional normals correspond to parallel directions.
Make sure each pair of line coefficients actually defines a nonzero normal
before normalizing it.
The perpendicular distance from a point x zero, y zero to the line A x plus B
y
plus C equal to zero is the absolute value of A x zero plus B y zero plus C
divided by square root of A squared plus B squared.
The denominator normalizes the normal vector and makes the answer independent
of multiplying the equation by a nonzero constant.
From point one, two to three x plus four y minus six equal to zero, the
numerator is five and the denominator is five, giving distance one.
A point on the line has distance zero.
For two parallel lines with exactly the same A and B coefficients, their
distance is the absolute difference of the constant terms divided by the same
normal length.
Thus three x plus four y minus six equal to zero and three x plus four y plus
four equal to zero are distance two apart.
First rescale proportional equations so their normal coefficients agree.
Subtracting unmatched constants from differently scaled equations would
produce
a meaningless distance.
Distance is nonnegative, so retain the absolute value even when a chosen
normal
orientation reverses.
The centroid of a nondegenerate triangle is the average of its three vertex
coordinates.
It is the intersection of the medians and divides each median in the ratio two
to one measured from the vertex.
The circumcentre is the intersection of perpendicular bisectors and is equally
distant from all three vertices.
The orthocentre is the intersection of altitudes, which pass through vertices
perpendicular to the opposite sides.
For the triangle with vertices zero, zero; six, zero; and zero, eight, the
centroid is two, eight thirds.
This triangle is right angled at the origin.
Its hypotenuse has midpoint three, four, which is the circumcentre, and the
circumradius is five.
The two coordinate axes are altitudes, so the orthocentre is the origin.
These three centres are different points.
In a general triangle, solve two perpendicular bisector equations for the
circumcentre and two altitude equations for the orthocentre.
Vertical or horizontal sides need their perpendicular directions handled
directly instead of using an undefined slope.
Collinear vertices do not form a nondegenerate triangle, so the usual finite
unique circumcentre construction is not available in that case.
A circle with centre h, k and positive radius r consists of points at distance
r from that centre.
Its standard equation is the square of x minus h plus the square of y minus k
equal to r squared.
Expanding leads to the general form x squared plus y squared plus two g x plus
two f y plus c equal to zero.
Completing the squares gives centre negative g, negative f and radius squared
g
squared plus f squared minus c.
For x squared plus y squared minus four x plus six y minus twelve equal to
zero, the centre is two, negative three.
Completing the squares yields the square of x minus two plus the square of y
plus three equal to twenty five, so the radius is five.
Check the sign of the radius squared: a positive value gives a real circle,
zero gives a single point, and a negative value gives no real points.
If the common nonzero coefficient of x squared and y squared is not one,
divide
the entire equation by it before reading g, f and c.
Equal quadratic coefficients alone do not guarantee a real positive radius
circle.
If the endpoints of a diameter are known, the centre is their midpoint and the
radius is half their distance.
For A at negative one, zero and B at three, zero, the midpoint is one, zero
and
the radius is two.
Thus the circle has equation the square of x minus one plus y squared equal to
four.
A useful direct diameter equation is x minus x one times x minus
x two, plus y minus y one times y minus y two equal to
zero.
In this example it becomes x plus one times x minus three, plus y squared
equal to zero, which expands to the same circle.
The direct form comes from the right angle subtended by a diameter, expressed
as a zero dot product for the two endpoint vectors from a point on the circle.
Verify that both endpoints satisfy the equation.
Distinct endpoints are required for a positive radius circle.
If the endpoints coincide, the algebra instead describes a zero radius point.
Do not mistake the endpoint distance for the radius; it is the full diameter
and must be halved.
To intersect a line and a circle, substitute one equation into the other and
solve the resulting quadratic or simpler equation.
For x squared plus y squared equal to twenty five and line y equal to three,
substitution gives x squared equal to sixteen.
The intersection points are negative four, three and four, three.
Their distance is eight, the chord length.
The perpendicular from the circle centre bisects the chord, giving the general
chord formula twice square root of r squared minus d squared, where d is the
centre to line distance.
Here r is five and d is three, so the half chord is four.
If d is less than r there are two intersections, if d equals r there is one
tangent contact, and if d exceeds r there is no real intersection.
The quadratic discriminant gives the same three cases when substitution
produces a genuine quadratic.
A vertical line can be substituted by fixing x directly.
Always substitute the candidate points back into both original equations,
since
roots of an incorrectly rearranged quadratic may not represent actual common
points.
A tangent to a real circle meets it at one point and is perpendicular to the
radius through that point.
On the circle x squared plus y squared equal to r squared, the tangent at an
actual circle point x one, y one has equation x x one plus y y one
equal to r squared.
At point three, four on the circle of radius five centred at the origin, the
tangent is three x plus four y equal to twenty five.
Its normal points along the radius, and its distance from the origin is twenty
five over five, or five, confirming tangency.
The point must lie on the circle before this formula can be used as the
tangent
at that point.
For a shifted centre, translate the coordinates first or use the radius as the
normal direction.
To decide whether a general line is tangent, compare the centre to line
distance with the radius.
This avoids solving for a repeated quadratic root.
Tangency is a useful supporting application of the line and circle methods;
the
point and distance checks prevent a memorized tangent formula being used at an
unrelated point.
A focus directrix description defines a conic through a fixed positive ratio.
The distance from a moving point P to the focus equals eccentricity e times
the
perpendicular distance from P to a fixed directrix line.
For positive e less than one, the nondegenerate conic is an ellipse.
For e equal to one it is a parabola, and for e greater than one it is a
hyperbola.
The circle is conventionally the eccentricity zero limiting case of an
ellipse;
do not insert e equal to zero into a fixed finite focus directrix description
and expect a circle, since that literal equation would give only the focus.
In standard centred conics, c denotes the centre to focus distance.
For an ellipse with semimajor length a and semiminor length b, c squared
equals
a squared minus b squared.
For a hyperbola with transverse semiaxis a and conjugate parameter b, c
squared
equals a squared plus b squared.
In both cases eccentricity is c over a.
Read the orientation and the role of a before computing c: for a hyperbola the
positive squared term, rather than the larger denominator, determines the
transverse axis.
For a positive, the parabola y squared equal to four a x opens to the right,
has vertex at the origin, focus a, zero, and directrix x equal to negative a.
Its axis is the x axis.
The latus rectum is the chord through the focus perpendicular to that axis.
Setting x equal to a gives y equal to positive or negative two a, so its
length
is four a.
In y squared equal to eight x, a is two, the focus is two, zero and the latus
rectum length is eight.
Changing the right hand side to negative four a x reflects the parabola left,
with focus negative a, zero and directrix x equal to a.
Swapping x and y produces the upward and downward forms x squared equal to
positive or negative four a y.
In each orientation the focus is on the opening side and the directrix on the
opposite side of the vertex.
Compare the coefficient with four a, not a alone, and keep the opening sign
separate from the positive focal length parameter.
A convenient parameter for y squared equal to four a x is x equal to a t
squared and y equal to two a t, with real t.
Substitution verifies the equation directly, and every point on this parabola
has such a parameter.
The tangent at that parameter has equation t y equal to x plus a t squared.
For y squared equal to eight x, a is two.
At t equal to one, the point is two, four and the tangent is y equal to x plus
two.
Substituting that line into the parabola produces a repeated root at the
contact point, confirming tangency.
At t equal to zero, the point is the vertex and the tangent formula gives x
equal to zero, a vertical line.
A slope expression that divides by t would miss that case, so the parameter
equation is more robust.
These tangent and parameter facts support the standard form rather than
replacing its focus and directrix definition.
Verify the point first, keep the sign of t to distinguish the two halves, and
avoid assuming that a vertical tangent has finite slope.
For the standard horizontal ellipse x squared over a squared plus y squared
over b squared equal to one, take a greater than b and both positive.
Its major axis has length two a along x, and its minor axis has length two b
along y.
The foci are positive and negative c, zero, with c squared equal to a squared
minus b squared.
Eccentricity is c over a.
For denominators twenty five and nine, a is five, b is three, c is four and e
is four fifths.
The major and minor axis lengths are ten and six.
The directrices are x equal to positive or negative a over e, giving positive
or negative twenty five fourths.
The latus rectum length is two b squared over a, or eighteen fifths.
If the larger denominator lies under y squared, the major axis is vertical and
the focus and directrix roles swap coordinates.
Equal positive denominators describe a circle, where the finite directrix
formula involving division by e is unavailable.
Check whether a requested quantity is a semiaxis or a full axis before giving
its numerical value.
For a horizontal hyperbola in the form x squared over a squared minus y
squared
over b squared equal to one, a and b are positive.
The vertices are positive and negative a, zero.
The foci are positive and negative c, zero, where c squared is a squared plus
b
squared.
Thus e equal to c over a is greater than one.
In x squared over nine minus y squared over sixteen equal to one, a is three,
b
is four, c is five and the foci are five units from the centre.
The asymptotes are y equal to positive or negative b over a times x, giving
slopes positive and negative four thirds.
The directrices are x equal to positive or negative a over e, or positive and
negative nine fifths.
The latus rectum length is two b squared over a, giving thirty two thirds.
For the vertical form y squared over a squared minus x squared over b squared
equal to one, the vertices and foci lie on y, and the asymptotes have slopes
positive and negative a over b.
The positive term determines the opening axis, regardless of which denominator
is larger.
Translations move standard conics without changing their lengths or
eccentricity.
Replace x by x minus h and y by y minus k to move a centred conic to centre h,
k.
The ellipse with the square of x minus two over twenty five plus the square of
y plus one over nine equal to one has centre two, negative one.
Its focal distance is four, so its foci are negative two, negative one and
six,
negative one.
For a translated right opening parabola, the square of y minus k equals four a
times x minus h.
Its vertex is h, k, its focus is h plus a, k, and its directrix is x equal to
h
minus a.
Completing squares helps convert an expanded equation into these forms.
Do not classify a curve solely from two visible squared terms without checking
the completed equation.
A sum of nonnegative squares equal to a negative number has no real points,
while equality to zero may give a single point.
State the centre or vertex, orientation and reality conditions first, then
compute distances or intersections from the normalized standard form.
